lesson.subtitle: Lesson 8 -- The Year-End Room
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Luiz Fernando da Silva | Lesson 8 -- The Year-End Room
lesson.grammar_point: passive voice, present and past simple

listenings.text: Luiz, it's Claire. The minutes from Tuesday have been circulated and your name is in them. Item four point four: the southern portfolio was delegated to the regional analyst. That is you. Item four point three: the revised limits were approved without objection. Nothing else about credit was changed. Item four point five is still open, because terms with two distributors are still being negotiated. And item nine: the year-end event was confirmed, and the regional teams are going to be invited. You should come.

Mister da Silva, this is Rui from the events team. The year-end room has been booked for the eleventh. Forty places. The invitations were sent this morning, so check your inbox. Three things are decided by the room and not by me. Dinner is served at eight. The tables are set for six people. And nobody is seated with their own team, which is done on purpose. If you need anything changed, it has to be requested by Friday.

vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: to send a document formally to somebody who will decide on it
to take somebody on as an employee
to give a task, and the authority for it, to somebody who reports to you
to say something officially, so that everybody hears it at the same time
the small group that oversees a company on behalf of its owners
to look at something again in order to judge it
to say officially that something may go ahead
to discuss terms until both sides can accept them

paras: Read the minutes of any board meeting in the world and you will notice something strange: almost nobody does anything. The budget is approved. The report was submitted. A new head of region has been hired. Actions happen, dates are recorded, and the person who decided disappears from the sentence. That is not laziness and it is not evasion. In a document that will be read in four countries by people who have never met, what matters is the decision and the date, not who happened to be holding the pen. English has a whole grammar for exactly that, and corporate life runs on it.

The same construction has a second, less innocent use, and it is worth being able to hear it. Mistakes were made removes the person from the sentence just as efficiently as the budget was approved does, and in that case the disappearance is the point. This is why the passive has a bad reputation with people who teach writing, and why the advice to avoid it is too simple. The question is never whether the sentence hides the actor. It is whether hiding the actor is honest in that particular sentence. A credit limit was approved on the fifteenth is a fact. A decision was taken to release the product is often somebody hoping you will not ask who took it.

And then there is the year-end party, which is the same building and the exact opposite of the same language. Legally the event is treated as an extension of the workplace, so it is organised as carefully as a meeting. Socially it is the one evening in the year when the grammar has to change back. Nobody wants to hear that the file was reviewed and the limit was raised. They want to hear that you read it on a Sunday, that you called the dealer yourself, and that you were wrong about him. On the page the actor disappears and the decision survives. At the table it is the other way round, and an analyst who cannot make that switch spends the whole evening sounding like a document.

reading.prompt: What is the main idea of the text?
choices: The passive voice should be avoided in business English because it hides responsibility.
Corporate documents remove the actor on purpose and that is usually honest, but the same grammar has to be switched off at a social event.
Board minutes are badly written because the people who write them are careless.
